name: Sustainability
answer: These measures show the carbon, water and energy sourcing behind a data center's operation. AI demand has made data centers one of the fastest growing users of electricity, so these figures are where climate commitments meet actual consumption.

metrics.line: Liters of water consumed by the facility, chiefly for evaporative cooling, per kilowatt-hour of IT energy delivered.
metrics.label: WUE, Water Usage Effectiveness

metrics.line: Kilograms of carbon dioxide emitted, from the grid mix and on-site generation, per kilowatt-hour of IT energy.
metrics.label: CUE, Carbon Usage Effectiveness

metrics.line: The share of facility consumption matched by renewable generation, reported either as annual matching through purchased certificates or as around-the-clock hourly matching.
metrics.label: Renewable energy utilization

reading.body:
Sustainability reporting for data centers comes down to three measures: water use per kilowatt-hour of IT energy, carbon per kilowatt-hour, and the share of consumption matched by renewables.

The pattern is that all three are ratios against IT energy delivered, not totals. That choice matters. A facility can grow its absolute electricity draw and absolute water consumption while WUE and CUE stay flat or improve, because the denominators grow too. Efficiency per unit of compute and total resource consumption are different claims, and only the first is captured here.

For AI specifically, the binding question is whether renewable matching is annual or hourly. Annual matching through purchased certificates can be satisfied by generation that does not coincide with when the load runs. Around-the-clock hourly matching cannot. The data names both methods without saying which a given facility uses, and the gap between them is where most of the disagreement about whether AI compute is clean actually sits.

What this does not cover: no facility, operator, region, or numeric value appears here, so nothing can be compared across sites or tracked over time. It also does not address grid capacity, interconnection, or land, which sit in sibling categories rather than this one.
